nodes.label: Wave Optics and Interference
nodes.note: Wave optics drops the ray picture and tracks phase, so interference, diffraction, and polarization follow from superposing wavefronts. Every result reduces to one path difference and one condition such as $$\Delta x = n\lambda$$.

nodes.label: Huygens' Principle
nodes.note: Every point on a primary wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets whose envelope forms the next wavefront. The construction rebuilds both laws of optics from geometry alone, starting from $$v = f\lambda$$.

nodes.label: Wavefronts and Wavelets
nodes.note: A wavefront is the locus of points in the same phase, and the ray is normal to it. Plane waves from a distant source travel at $$v = \frac{c}{\mu}$$ in a medium of index $$\mu$$.

nodes.label: Reflection from Huygens' Construction
nodes.note: Comparing equal-time secondary wavelets on both sides of the interface tilts the new wavefront by the same amount the ray turns. This recovers the law of reflection: $$i = r$$.

nodes.label: Refraction from Huygens' Construction
nodes.note: Different wave speeds on the two sides rotate the wavefront and bend the ray. The construction gives Snell's law as a speed ratio: $$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$$.

nodes.label: Wavefront Shaping by Elements
nodes.note: Lenses and mirrors bend wavefronts without changing their frequency, so a plane wavefront emerges as a converging one. A converging wavefront of radius $$R$$ focuses at the centre of curvature, giving $$f = \frac{R}{2}$$ for a mirror.

nodes.label: Superposition and Coherence
nodes.note: Displacements add linearly while the waves overlap, and the constant phase difference between them decides the pattern. The resultant amplitude follows $$R^2 = a_1^2 + a_2^2 + 2a_1a_2\cos\phi$$.

nodes.label: Resultant of Two Harmonic Vibrations
nodes.note: Two same-frequency oscillations combine into one oscillation of the same frequency. The amplitude is $$R = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + 2a_1a_2\cos\phi}$$, which lies between $$|a_1 - a_2|$$ and $$a_1 + a_2$$.

nodes.label: Intensity and Phase Difference
nodes.note: Intensity adds with a cross term set by the phase difference: $$I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$$. For equal sources this collapses to $$I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Constructive and Destructive Conditions
nodes.note: Maxima need whole-wavelength path difference and minima need a half-odd number of them: $$\Delta x = n\lambda$$ bright, $$\Delta x = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$ dark. In phase language these are $$\phi = 2n\pi$$ and $$\phi = (2n + 1)\pi$$.

nodes.label: Coherence and Energy Sharing
nodes.note: Coherent sources share a fixed phase relation, which only division of a single wavefront or division of amplitude can guarantee. Time-averaging the interference term gives $$\langle I \rangle = I_1 + I_2$$, so energy is redistributed, never created.

nodes.label: Young's Double Slit Experiment
nodes.note: Two slits fed by one wavefront act as coherent sources separated by $$d$$ and screened at distance $$D$$. Brightness on the screen is decided by $$\Delta x = \frac{yd}{D}$$.

nodes.label: Path Difference Geometry
nodes.note: For a distant screen the extra path from one slit is the projection of the slit separation: $$\Delta x = d\sin\theta$$. With $$D \gg d$$ this becomes $$\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta = \frac{y}{D}$$.

nodes.label: Fringe Positions and Width
nodes.note: Bright fringes sit at $$y_n = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}$$ and dark ones halfway between them. Consecutive fringes are separated by the fringe width $$\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$$.

nodes.label: Intensity Pattern on the Screen
nodes.note: Substituting the path difference into the intensity law gives a smooth cosine-squared profile. $$I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi y d}{\lambda D}\right)$$, so minima are perfectly dark for equal amplitudes.

nodes.label: Maximum Number of Fringes
nodes.note: The order cannot exceed the geometric limit $$|\sin\theta| \le 1$$, so $$n_{max} = \left\lfloor \frac{d}{\lambda} \right\rfloor$$. The screen therefore holds about $$N = 2n_{max} + 1$$ bright fringes in total.

nodes.label: YDSE Immersed in a Medium
nodes.note: Filling the apparatus shortens the wavelength, so the whole pattern contracts toward the centre. $$\lambda_{med} = \frac{\lambda_{air}}{\mu}$$ implies $$\beta_{med} = \frac{\beta_{air}}{\mu}$$.

nodes.label: White Light Fringes
nodes.note: At the centre every wavelength has zero path difference, so the central fringe stays white. Since $$y_n = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}$$ depends on colour, higher orders spread into a spectrum and fade.

nodes.label: Optical Path and Slab Shifts
nodes.note: Light travels slower in matter, so a slab makes a ray take the time of a longer vacuum path. Optical path is therefore $$L_{opt} = \mu x$$.

nodes.label: Optical Path Length
nodes.note: A geometric length $$x$$ in index $$\mu$$ delays light as much as $$\mu x$$ in vacuum: $$L_{opt} = \mu x$$. The transit time over that length is $$t = \frac{\mu x}{c}$$.

nodes.label: Fringe Shift by a Dielectric Slab
nodes.note: A slab of thickness $$t$$ and index $$\mu$$ in one arm adds optical path $$(\mu - 1)t$$ and drags the pattern toward that slit. The central fringe moves by $$\Delta y = \frac{(\mu - 1)t D}{d}$$, shifting $$N = \frac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$$ fringes.

nodes.label: Slabs Before Both Slits
nodes.note: Equal slabs in both arms add the same delay to each path, so the difference never changes. The pattern stays put: $$\Delta y = 0$$. Unequal slabs instead give $$\Delta y = \frac{[(\mu_1 - 1)t_1 - (\mu_2 - 1)t_2]D}{d}$$.

nodes.label: Counting Shifted Fringes
nodes.note: Fringes shift by one whenever the added optical path reaches a wavelength, so counting shift equals counting extra waves. The count is $$N = \frac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$$ for one slabbed arm.

nodes.label: Wavefront Division Experiments
nodes.note: These experiments slice one wavefront into pieces, which guarantees coherence without splitting intensity by amplitude. The screen pattern is always $$\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$$ with an effective source separation $$d$$.

nodes.label: Fresnel's Biprism
nodes.note: A shallow prism pair creates two interfering virtual images of one narrow source. Their separation is $$d = 2a(\mu - 1)\alpha$$, so the fringes follow $$\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$$.

nodes.label: Lloyd's Single Mirror
nodes.note: A plane mirror makes a virtual source from the same real source, so the two beams are automatically coherent. Reflection adds a half-wave, giving $$\Delta x = 2d\sin\theta + \frac{\lambda}{2}$$ and a dark edge along the mirror.

nodes.label: Building a Coherent Pair
nodes.note: Splitting one wavefront keeps the two beams locked to the same source phase, unlike two independent lamps. The fringe contrast then reaches its ideal value $$\frac{I_{max} - I_{min}}{I_{max} + I_{min}} = 1$$.

nodes.label: Thin Film Interference
nodes.note: A film splits one ray into a reflected and a refracted pair that later recombine, dividing amplitude rather than wavefront. Path difference comes from the double traverse $$2\mu d\cos r$$.

nodes.label: Stokes' Phase Reversal
nodes.note: Reflection at a denser boundary flips the phase by $$\pi$$, which counts as an extra $$\frac{\lambda}{2}$$ of path. Reflection from a rarer boundary and every transmission suffer no such jump.

nodes.label: Reflected Bright and Dark Conditions
nodes.note: Counting the half-wave from the top reflection flips the usual rule: bright in reflection needs $$2\mu d\cos r = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$. Dark in reflection follows $$2\mu d\cos r = n\lambda$$.

nodes.label: Transmitted Light and Complementarity
nodes.note: Transmitted rays pick up no boundary phase shift, so their conditions are the exact inverse of the reflected ones: $$2\mu d\cos r = n\lambda$$ is bright. Whatever one beam loses the other gains, keeping energy consistent.

nodes.label: Colours of Soap Films
nodes.note: Under white light each thickness and viewing angle selects a different wavelength, painting the film in bands. Selection obeys $$2\mu d\cos r = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$ as $$d$$ and $$r$$ vary across the film.

nodes.label: Wedge Film Fringes
nodes.note: A wedge of small angle $$\theta$$ has thickness growing linearly along it, so equal-thickness fringes are straight and equally spaced. The spacing is $$\beta = \frac{\lambda}{2\mu\theta}$$ for near-normal viewing.

nodes.label: Single-Slit Diffraction
nodes.note: An aperture comparable to the wavelength spreads light into the geometric shadow, making the central band the brightest. Edge-to-edge path difference for a slit of width $$a$$ is $$\Delta x = a\sin\theta$$.

nodes.label: Diffraction Minima
nodes.note: The slit splits into pairs of half-wave zones that cancel whenever the edge path difference is a full wavelength. Dark fringes obey $$a\sin\theta = n\lambda$$ for $$n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$.

nodes.label: Secondary Maxima
nodes.note: Between neighbouring minima one uncompensated zone survives and makes a weak bright band. The condition is $$a\sin\theta = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$$, and peak intensities fall as $$1 : 0.045 : 0.016 : \dots$$.

nodes.label: Central Maximum Width
nodes.note: The central band is bounded by the first minima on both sides, so it is twice as wide as any other band. Its linear width on a screen at $$D$$ is $$\beta_0 = \frac{2\lambda D}{a}$$.

nodes.label: Diffraction Intensity Profile
nodes.note: Fraunhofer intensity is the squared sinc of the slit phase parameter: $$I = I_0\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2$$. The parameter is $$\alpha = \frac{\pi a\sin\theta}{\lambda}$$, and $$\alpha = 0$$ gives the central peak.

nodes.label: Slit Width Trade-off
nodes.note: Narrowing the slit spreads the pattern because first minima satisfy $$\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{a}$$. Interference fringes stay fixed while diffraction fringes widen, so diffraction sets the visible envelope.

nodes.label: Resolution and Polarization
nodes.note: Diffraction blurs point sources and polarization exposes the transverse character of light. Rayleigh's criterion turns blur into a number: $$d\theta = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}$$.

nodes.label: Rayleigh's Criterion
nodes.note: Two sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other. A circular aperture of diameter $$D$$ then limits angular separation to $$d\theta = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}$$.

nodes.label: Microscope Resolving Limit
nodes.note: A microscope separates points at a minimum distance set by numerical aperture $$NA = \mu\sin\theta$$. The limit is $$\Delta d = \frac{1.22\lambda}{2\mu\sin\theta}$$, so resolving power is $$RP = \frac{1}{\Delta d}$$.

nodes.label: Brewster's Law
nodes.note: At the polarizing angle the reflected ray is fully plane-polarized and stands perpendicular to the refracted ray. That geometry gives $$\tan i_p = \mu$$, so the reflected and refracted beams are 90 degrees apart.

nodes.label: Malus's Law
nodes.note: Only the analyzer-parallel component of the electric vector gets through, so intensity falls with the squared cosine: $$I = I_0\cos^2\theta$$. An ideal polarizer cuts unpolarized light to half: $$I = \frac{I_0}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Transverse Nature of Light
nodes.note: Polarization is impossible for longitudinal waves, so it proves the electric oscillation is transverse to propagation. The wave speed follows from vacuum constants: $$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$$.
